result:
Solution 3 gives 12, which my check supports, though I did not prove the upper bound.

**Why 12 looks achievable.** I checked Solution 3's construction: assign each assistant its own edge, with slower assistants on edges nearer the start. Each assistant first transits to its edge and then bounces on it forever.
- Assistants moving outward from the start vertex at the same time on a shared edge all go the same way at different speeds. The faster one stays ahead, so they never meet in the interior of an edge.
- A fast transiter clears a shared edge long before a slower bouncer first comes back to it. For example, the speed-1024 assistant crosses edge 100–110 around t ≈ 1/1024, while the speed-16 bouncer only arrives at t = 1/16.
- Once every assistant is bouncing, each edge carries exactly one bouncer, so no interior collisions occur.

This construction appears valid, so n ≥ 12.

**Why more than 12 looks implausible.** Two assistants bouncing on the same edge at different speeds always meet at an interior point. For example, speeds 2 and 4 starting together meet at 1/2 after the faster one turns around. That suggests at most one bouncer per edge, hence at most 12. Solution 3's argument for this step is only sketched, and I did not prove it independently.

**Why the others fail.**
- Solution 1 claims 8, but the construction above already gives 12.
- Solution 2 claims 3, but its argument only considers shared directed cycles and dismisses bouncing strategies without justification. The 12-edge construction contradicts it.

CHOICE: 3
